topics.title: Dielectrics and induced dipoles
topics.idea: A dielectric can respond to an electric field without allowing charges to travel through the whole sample.
topics.result: $\mathbf p=\alpha\mathbf E_{\rm local}$ in the weak-field isotropic model.
topics.explain: A nonpolar atom begins with coincident charge centres. The field shifts the positive centre with E and the negative centre against E.::Opposite charges feel opposite forces.;;The displacement stops when the internal restoring force balances the external force.::A stable atom is bound.;;The induced moment is proportional to the local field for small displacements.::A linear approximation is valid near equilibrium.
topics.trap: Do not confuse one atom's polarizability $\alpha$ with a bulk susceptibility $\chi_e$.
topics.check: Does a neutral atom need a net charge to become a dipole?=>No. Separation of its positive and negative charge centres is sufficient.

topics.title: Permanent dipoles: torque and force
topics.idea: A uniform field turns a permanent dipole; a nonuniform field can also pull it.
topics.result: $\boldsymbol\tau=\mathbf p\times\mathbf E$, $U=-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf E$; for a fixed dipole, $\mathbf F=(\mathbf p\cdot\nabla)\mathbf E$.
topics.explain: The two forces are $+q\mathbf E$ and $-q\mathbf E$. In a uniform field they cancel as forces.::Both charges see the same E.;;Their moments add to $pE\sin\theta$.::The forces act at different positions.;;If E changes across the dipole, subtract the two local fields and keep the first spatial derivative.::The dipole is small compared with the scale of variation.
topics.trap: For an induced dipole, substituting a field-dependent p directly into $U=-pE$ misses the work of inducing it.
topics.check: Which orientation has minimum permanent-dipole energy?=>Parallel: $U=-pE$.

topics.title: Polarization as a density
topics.idea: Polarization is the average electric dipole moment contained in a unit volume.
topics.explain: Add the dipole vectors in a small macroscopic volume.::Directions matter as well as the number of molecules.;;Divide by that volume.::This converts a collection of moments into a local material field.;;Random directions can give P=0 even when every molecule has a permanent moment.::Opposite vector contributions cancel.
topics.trap: P is not total charge density and is not the same as the electric field.
topics.check: If number density doubles at fixed aligned moment p, what happens to P?=>It doubles: $P=np$.

topics.title: Bound charge and the field of polarization
topics.idea: A collection of dipoles can be replaced, for field calculations, by equivalent surface and volume charges.
topics.explain: Neighbouring positive and negative ends cancel in the bulk when P is uniform.::Only unmatched ends remain at faces.;;Project P onto the outward face normal to find $\sigma_b$.::Only dipoles crossing that face contribute.;;For varying P, an imbalance also remains within each tiny volume: $\rho_b=-\nabla\cdot\mathbf P$.::Outward-growing dipole moment leaves negative bound charge locally.;;Compute V from these equivalent charges, then $\mathbf E=-\nabla V$.::They produce the same external and macroscopic internal field as the dipoles.
topics.trap: The surface normal must point out of the polarized object; reversing it reverses $\sigma_b$.
topics.check: Uniform P points right in a slab. Which face is positive?=>The right face, where the outward normal is parallel to P.

topics.title: Displacement and free charge
topics.idea: D packages the material polarization so that its flux counts only free charge.
topics.result: $\mathbf D=\epsilon_0\mathbf E+\mathbf P$; $\nabla\cdot\mathbf D=\rho_f$; $\oint\mathbf D\cdot d\mathbf a=Q_f$.
topics.explain: Gauss's law for E counts total charge: $\epsilon_0\nabla\cdot\mathbf E=\rho_f+\rho_b$.::Both bound and free charges make E.;;Insert $\rho_b=-\nabla\cdot\mathbf P$ and move that term to the left.::This groups the unknown material response with E.;;Define the grouped field as D.::Its divergence then has only the free source.
topics.trap: D is not always determined by free charges alone: boundary conditions and material geometry also matter.
topics.check: If a Gaussian surface encloses no free charge, must D vanish everywhere?=>No. Its net flux is zero; the local vector can be nonzero.

topics.title: Electric boundary conditions
topics.idea: A thin pillbox and a tiny loop tell us which field components can jump at a surface.
topics.result: $D_{2n}-D_{1n}=\sigma_f$; $\mathbf E_{2t}=\mathbf E_{1t}$ in electrostatics. Normal n points from medium 1 to 2.
topics.explain: Shrink a pillbox straddling the interface: the side flux vanishes and the two caps give the normal jump.::Gauss's law encloses the free surface charge.;;Shrink a rectangular loop across the interface.::Electrostatic circulation is zero.;;Only the two tangential sides survive, so tangential E is continuous.::The connecting short sides vanish with loop height.
topics.trap: Normal E need not be continuous. With no free surface charge, normal D is continuous.
topics.check: At an interface with no free charge and $\epsilon_2=2\epsilon_1$, how do normal fields compare?=>$E_{2n}=E_{1n}/2$.

topics.title: Linear dielectrics and capacitors
topics.idea: For an isotropic linear dielectric the polarization follows the macroscopic electric field.
topics.explain: Insert the linear P relation into $D=\epsilon_0E+P$.::The material contribution is proportional to E.;;Factor E to identify the permittivity.::Vacuum and material response add.;;For a fully filled parallel-plate capacitor, $D=Q_f/A$, $V=Ed$, hence $C=\epsilon A/d$.::Symmetry makes the field nearly uniform away from edges.
topics.trap: State whether the battery remains connected. Fixed V and fixed Q lead to different energy changes.
topics.check: If $\chi_e=3$, what is the relative permittivity?=>$\epsilon_r=4$.

topics.title: Magnetic response of atoms
topics.idea: Orbital and spin magnetic moments explain different responses to applied fields.
topics.result: Diamagnets: $\chi_m<0$; paramagnets: small $\chi_m>0$; ferromagnets: strong, history-dependent response.
topics.explain: A current loop is a magnetic dipole. Electrons also have intrinsic spin moments.::Both contribute to atomic magnetism.;;An applied field changes orbital motion, inducing an opposing contribution.::This gives diamagnetism.;;Existing moments tend to align, but thermal motion disrupts that order.::This gives weak paramagnetism in suitable materials.
topics.trap: Spin is an intrinsic quantum property, not literally a tiny charged sphere rotating classically.
topics.check: Why does heating usually weaken paramagnetic alignment?=>More thermal disorder competes with field alignment.

topics.title: Magnetization and magnetic torque
topics.idea: M measures magnetic dipole moment per volume, just as P measures electric dipole moment per volume.
topics.result: $\mathbf M=\text{magnetic moment}/\text{volume}$ in A/m; $\boldsymbol\tau=\mathbf m\times\mathbf B$.
topics.explain: Sum the atomic magnetic moments as vectors, then divide by volume.::Antialigned moments cancel.;;For a small loop, $m=IA$.::Current and loop area determine its dipole moment.;;In a uniform field its torque turns m toward B.::Opposite forces on opposite sides form a couple.
topics.trap: M has units A/m, while magnetic moment m has units A m².
topics.check: A moment $0.02$ A m² occupies $10^{-4}$ m³. What is M?=>$200$ A/m if uniformly aligned.

topics.title: Bound currents and magnetized objects
topics.idea: Tiny current loops cancel internally but leave equivalent currents at surfaces and where M varies.
topics.result: $\mathbf K_b=\mathbf M\times\hat{\mathbf n}$ in A/m; $\mathbf J_b=\nabla\times\mathbf M$ in A/m².
topics.explain: Adjacent loops have opposing currents on their common edges.::Uniform bulk contributions cancel.;;Loops at the outer edge have no neighbour to cancel them.::They form a surface current sheet.;;A nonuniform loop density leaves a bulk remainder.::This is represented by curl M.;;Use the ordinary magnetic field laws for these equivalent currents.::They reproduce the macroscopic field of the magnetization.;;Define vector potential A by $B=\nabla\times A$. For localized steady sources, add $\mu_0J_b\,d\tau/(4\pi\mathcal R)$ and $\mu_0K_b\,da/(4\pi\mathcal R)$ over the body and surface to obtain A, where $\mathcal R$ is distance to the observation point.::Equivalent bound currents also act as sources for the magnetic vector potential.
topics.trap: The syllabus asks for physical interpretation of bound currents; the full microscopic derivation is not required.
topics.check: For uniform M inside an object, what is the bulk bound current?=>Zero, although its surface current can remain.

topics.title: The auxiliary field H
topics.idea: H removes the bound-current contribution from the magnetostatic circulation law.
topics.result: $\mathbf H=\mathbf B/\mu_0-\mathbf M$; $\nabla\times\mathbf H=\mathbf J_f$; $\oint\mathbf H\cdot d\mathbf l=I_f$.
topics.explain: Start with $\nabla\times\mathbf B=\mu_0(\mathbf J_f+\mathbf J_b)$.::Both kinds of steady current produce B.;;Substitute $\mathbf J_b=\nabla\times\mathbf M$.::M represents the bound current.;;Move curl M to the left and define H.::The remaining source is free current.
topics.trap: H is not generally curl-free, and $H=0$ does not imply $B=0$ inside a magnet.
topics.check: An ideal long solenoid has n turns per metre and free current I. What is H inside?=>$H=nI$ along the axis.

topics.title: Magnetic susceptibility and permeability
topics.idea: A linear isotropic magnetic medium has magnetization proportional to H.
topics.explain: Use $\mathbf B=\mu_0(\mathbf H+\mathbf M)$.::This is the definition of H rearranged.;;Insert $\mathbf M=\chi_m\mathbf H$ and factor H.::Linearity makes a scalar permeability possible.;;Apply this only over a range where the material response is approximately linear.::Ferromagnetic response can depend on both field and history.
topics.trap: The electric relation uses P proportional to E; the magnetic convention uses M proportional to H.
topics.check: If $\chi_m=-10^{-5}$, is $\mu$ above or below $\mu_0$?=>Slightly below.

topics.title: Ferromagnetism and memory
topics.idea: Domains can align cooperatively and retain alignment after the applied field is removed.
topics.result: Remanence is the remaining magnetization; coercive field is the reverse field needed to bring magnetization to zero on a hysteresis branch.
topics.explain: Within a domain many moments align.::Neighbouring moments interact cooperatively.;;Changing an applied field moves domain walls and rotates moments.::Domains favourable to the field grow.;;Removing the field does not retrace the initial path.::Pinning and collective rearrangement make the response history dependent.;;Heating above the Curie temperature destroys spontaneous ferromagnetic order.::Thermal disorder overcomes the ordered state.
topics.trap: A single constant susceptibility cannot describe an entire hysteresis loop. B-H and M-H coercive definitions need their own axes.
topics.check: Why use a soft magnetic core in an AC device?=>Its narrow hysteresis loop reduces cycle losses.

questions.prompt: How can an electrically neutral dielectric respond to a static electric field?
questions.answer: Its positive and negative charge centres shift slightly relative to one another, or existing molecular dipoles turn. Charges remain bound rather than crossing the whole material.
questions.final: Neutrality does not prevent polarization.

questions.prompt: Define atomic polarizability and give its SI unit.
questions.answer: For a weak local field, $\mathbf p=\alpha\mathbf E_{\rm local}$. Thus $[\alpha]=(\mathrm{C\,m})/(\mathrm{V/m})=\mathrm{C\,m^2/V}$. The atom is isotropic in this scalar linear model; α describes an individual atom rather than the whole sample.
questions.final: Polarizability is induced dipole moment per unit local field.

questions.prompt: A permanent dipole has moment $2\times10^{-29}$ C m in a field $3\times10^5$ V/m at 30°. Find the torque magnitude.
questions.answer: $\tau=pE\sin\theta=(2\times10^{-29})(3\times10^5)(0.5)=3\times10^{-24}$ N m. The torque turns p toward E.
questions.final: $\tau=3\times10^{-24}$ N m.

questions.prompt: Which orientation of a permanent dipole in a uniform field is stable? Use energy.
questions.answer: $U=-pE\cos\theta$ is minimum at $\theta=0$. A small angular displacement produces a restoring torque. The antiparallel orientation is an energy maximum.
questions.final: Parallel alignment is stable.

questions.prompt: Define polarization and distinguish it from dipole moment.
questions.answer: P is electric dipole moment per unit volume (C/m²). The moment p of one dipole has units C m. P is a bulk average and can vanish through random orientation.
questions.final: $\mathbf P=\Delta\mathbf p/\Delta\tau$.

questions.prompt: A material has $5\times10^{27}$ aligned dipoles per m³, each of moment $2\times10^{-30}$ C m. Find P.
questions.answer: Multiply moment per dipole by dipoles per volume: $P=np=10^{-2}$ C/m², directed along the common dipole direction.

questions.prompt: A face normal makes 60° with uniform $\mathbf P$, whose magnitude is 0.04 C/m². Find the bound surface charge density.
questions.answer: $\sigma_b=\mathbf P\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}=P\cos60^\circ=0.020$ C/m². This sign assumes the stated outward normal.
questions.final: $\sigma_b=+0.020$ C/m².

questions.prompt: What is the physical interpretation of bound charges? Include the case of uniform polarization.
questions.answer: Polarization separates positive and negative charge within atoms or molecules, leaving unmatched dipole ends at boundaries and wherever the dipole density varies. These charges remain associated with the material, unlike mobile free charge. For uniform P, $\rho_b=0$ inside but $\sigma_b=P\cdot\hat n$ may remain at its surface.
questions.final: Bound charges are the macroscopic result of displaced or aligned microscopic dipoles.

questions.prompt: Define electric displacement and state its SI unit.
questions.answer: $\mathbf D=\epsilon_0\mathbf E+\mathbf P$. Both terms have units C/m². Its closed-surface flux equals enclosed free charge.
questions.final: D is measured in C/m².

questions.prompt: Which charge appears in Gauss's law for D, and which appears in Gauss's law for E?
questions.answer: D flux counts $Q_f$. The electric field law is $\epsilon_0\oint\mathbf E\cdot d\mathbf a=Q_f+Q_b$. Bound charge is still physically present.
questions.final: D counts free charge; E counts total charge.

questions.prompt: State the boundary condition for the normal component of D, with your normal convention.
questions.answer: Let n point from medium 1 to 2. Then $(\mathbf D_2-\mathbf D_1)\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}=\sigma_f$. This follows from a thin Gaussian pillbox.
questions.final: $D_{2n}-D_{1n}=\sigma_f$.

questions.prompt: Why is tangential E continuous across an electrostatic interface?
questions.answer: The electrostatic circulation $\oint\mathbf E\cdot d\mathbf l$ is zero. For a shrinking rectangular loop crossing the surface only its tangential sides survive, so $E_{2t}=E_{1t}$.
questions.final: Tangential E has no electrostatic jump.

questions.prompt: A linear dielectric has $\epsilon_r=5$. Find its electric susceptibility.
questions.answer: $\epsilon_r=1+\chi_e$, so $\chi_e=4$. Both relative permittivity and susceptibility are dimensionless.

questions.prompt: A capacitor stays connected to an ideal battery while a dielectric completely fills it. How do capacitance and free charge change?
questions.answer: For unchanged geometry, C increases by $\epsilon_r$. The battery fixes V, so $Q=CV$ also increases by $\epsilon_r$. Away from edges $E=V/d$ is unchanged.
questions.final: Both C and Q multiply by $\epsilon_r$.

questions.prompt: Distinguish paramagnets and diamagnets.
questions.answer: Diamagnets have a weak induced response opposing the applied field, with $\chi_m<0$ and $\mu_r<1$. Paramagnets have pre-existing moments that partially align with the field, giving small $\chi_m>0$ and $\mu_r>1$. Thermal disorder competes with paramagnetic alignment.
questions.final: Diamagnets oppose weakly; paramagnets align weakly.

questions.prompt: Why does a paramagnet have weak alignment rather than perfect alignment at ordinary temperature?
questions.answer: Permanent atomic moments tend to align with an applied field, but thermal agitation disorders them. The resulting average alignment is small and normally decreases when temperature rises at fixed weak field.
questions.final: Field alignment competes with thermal disorder.

questions.prompt: Define magnetic vector potential. How can it describe the field of a magnetized object?
questions.answer: The vector potential A is defined by $\mathbf B=\nabla\times\mathbf A$ and has units T m. In magnetostatics a localized magnetized object can be replaced by $\mathbf J_b=\nabla\times M$ and $\mathbf K_b=M\times\hat n$ in the usual current-source potential integrals. A is not unique: adding a gradient leaves its curl unchanged.
questions.final: B is curl A; equivalent bound currents may be used as A sources.

questions.prompt: Discuss briefly the bound currents in a magnetized medium, emphasizing their physical interpretation.
questions.answer: Microscopic magnetic dipoles can be modelled as current loops. Opposite currents on shared interior edges cancel for uniform M, leaving a surface current $K_b=M\times\hat n$. A spatially nonuniform magnetization can also leave $J_b=\nabla\times M$ in the bulk. These are equivalent macroscopic currents, not freely drifting conduction carriers.
questions.final: Uncancelled microscopic loops produce bound surface and volume currents.
tags: Legacy PYQ N25 Q18 · adapted marks

questions.prompt: Define H and state its magnetostatic circulation law.
questions.answer: $\mathbf H=\mathbf B/\mu_0-\mathbf M$. Its circulation is $\oint\mathbf H\cdot d\mathbf l=I_{f,\rm enc}$, using the right-hand orientation of the loop and current.
questions.final: Only enclosed free current appears in the H circulation law.

questions.prompt: Define magnetic susceptibility and relate it to relative permeability for a linear isotropic material.
questions.answer: Magnetic susceptibility is the dimensionless coefficient $\chi_m$ in $\mathbf M=\chi_m\mathbf H$. Since $B=\mu_0(H+M)$, $\mu_r=1+\chi_m$. For $\chi_m=0.002$, $\mu_r=1.002$. Ferromagnets need not obey one constant susceptibility.
questions.final: Magnetic susceptibility measures magnetization per unit H in the linear regime.

questions.prompt: Explain remanence, coercivity and the role of domain behaviour in an M-H hysteresis loop.
questions.answer: A ferromagnet contains domains with cooperative moment alignment.::Domains need not initially point in the same direction.;;Applied H moves walls and rotates domains.::Favourable orientations grow.;;After H returns to zero, pinning can leave nonzero M, called remanence.::The path depends on previous magnetic history.;;A reverse H is needed to reduce M to zero; its magnitude on that branch is the coercivity.::The two intercepts describe different properties.;;A narrow loop suits repeated cycling, whereas substantial coercivity helps a permanent magnet retain its state.::Applications depend on loss and resistance to demagnetization.
questions.final: Remanence measures retained M; coercivity measures the required reverse H.

questions.prompt: Explain the effect of heating a ferromagnet through the Curie temperature, and distinguish the result from diamagnetism.
questions.answer: Below the Curie temperature, interactions can maintain spontaneous alignment within domains.::Cooperative order survives thermal fluctuations.;;Raising temperature increases disorder and reduces spontaneous magnetization.::Thermal agitation competes with ordering interactions.;;Above the transition, spontaneous ferromagnetic order disappears and the material is paramagnetic.::It may still align weakly in an applied field.;;This is not diamagnetism: a paramagnetic response is positive and comes from existing moments, whereas the diamagnetic contribution opposes the field.::The microscopic mechanisms differ.
questions.final: Above its Curie temperature a ferromagnet loses spontaneous order and becomes paramagnetic.

questions.prompt: Model an atom as a point nucleus +q in a uniform spherical cloud −q of radius a. Derive its polarizability for a small nucleus displacement d.
questions.answer: The cloud density is $-3q/(4\pi a^3)$ and its interior field at displacement d is $-qd/(4\pi\epsilon_0a^3)$.::Gauss's law for a uniform sphere gives a field proportional to radius.;;At equilibrium $E=qd/(4\pi\epsilon_0a^3)$.::The applied and restoring forces cancel.;;Use $p=qd$ to obtain $p=4\pi\epsilon_0a^3E$.::Dipole moment is charge times separation.
questions.final: $\alpha=4\pi\epsilon_0a^3$ in this classical model.

questions.prompt: A fixed dipole $\mathbf p=p\hat{\mathbf x}$ is in $\mathbf E=kx^2\hat{\mathbf x}$. Find its force at x. Is there a torque?
questions.answer: The positive and negative ends sample different fields. To first order $F_x=p\,dE_x/dx$.::Subtract their two electric forces.;;Since $d(kx^2)/dx=2kx$, $\mathbf F=2pkx\hat{\mathbf x}$.::p is fixed, so only the field is differentiated.;;The torque is zero because p and E are collinear.::Their cross product vanishes.
questions.final: $\mathbf F=2pkx\hat{\mathbf x}$; $\boldsymbol\tau=0$.

questions.prompt: A sphere of radius R has $\mathbf P=a\mathbf r$ inside and zero outside. Find its bound charge densities and total bound charge.
questions.answer: $\nabla\cdot\mathbf r=3$, hence $\rho_b=-3a$.::Each Cartesian coordinate contributes one derivative.;;At $r=R$, $\sigma_b=\mathbf P\cdot\hat{\mathbf r}=aR$.::The sphere's normal is radial.;;$Q_{b,v}=(-3a)(4\pi R^3/3)=-4\pi aR^3$ and $Q_{b,s}=aR(4\pi R^2)=4\pi aR^3$.::Integrate the constant densities over volume and area.
questions.final: $\rho_b=-3a$, $\sigma_b=aR$; total bound charge is zero.

questions.prompt: An infinite slab is uniformly polarized perpendicular to its faces, with no free charge. Find E inside and outside.
questions.answer: The faces carry $-P$ and $+P$.::Use outward normals in $\sigma_b=\mathbf P\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}$.;;Each infinite sheet produces field magnitude $P/(2\epsilon_0)$.::Apply Gauss's law to one sheet.;;Between the sheets the fields add from positive to negative, opposing P; outside they cancel.::Superpose the two sheet fields.
questions.final: Inside $\mathbf E=-\mathbf P/\epsilon_0$; outside E=0.

questions.target: Line free charge in a dielectric
questions.prompt: A long straight wire with uniform free line charge λ is surrounded by rubber insulation out to radius a. Find the electric displacement, and state E if the rubber has permittivity ε and the exterior is vacuum.
questions.answer: Assume an infinitely long wire and cylindrical symmetry. A coaxial Gaussian cylinder of radius s and length ℓ has constant radial D on its curved face.::Translation and rotation symmetry remove axial and angular variation.;;The cap flux is zero, and curved flux is $D(2\pi s\ell)$.::D is radial.;;Enclosed free charge is $\lambda\ell$, so $D=\lambda/(2\pi s)$.::Gauss's law for D counts free charge only.;;Thus D has the same expression in rubber and outside. In rubber, $E=D/\epsilon$; outside, $E=D/\epsilon_0$.::The constitutive relation changes at s=a even though free-charge flux does not.
questions.final: $\mathbf D=\lambda\hat s/(2\pi s)$ outside the wire; E changes with the local permittivity.

questions.prompt: At an uncharged interface between isotropic dielectrics, derive the relation between field angles $\theta_1,\theta_2$ measured from the normal.
questions.answer: Tangential continuity gives $E_1\sin\theta_1=E_2\sin\theta_2$.::Electrostatic circulation vanishes.;;Normal D continuity gives $\epsilon_1E_1\cos\theta_1=\epsilon_2E_2\cos\theta_2$.::There is no free surface charge.;;Divide the first equation by the second.::Eliminate the field magnitudes.
questions.final: $\tan\theta_2/\tan\theta_1=\epsilon_2/\epsilon_1$ where the ratio is defined.

questions.prompt: A fully filled parallel-plate capacitor has area $0.010$ m², separation 1 mm and $\epsilon_r=4$. At 100 V find C, free Q and P.
questions.answer: $C=\epsilon_0\epsilon_rA/d=3.542\times10^{-10}$ F.::Ignore fringe fields.;;$Q_f=CV=3.542\times10^{-8}$ C and $E=V/d=10^5$ V/m.::The battery sets the potential difference.;;$P=\epsilon_0(\epsilon_r-1)E=2.656\times10^{-6}$ C/m².::Use the linear constitutive law.

questions.prompt: A charged capacitor is disconnected from its battery before a dielectric of relative permittivity k is inserted fully. Derive the ratios of V and stored energy.
questions.answer: Isolation fixes the free plate charge Q.::There is no route for charge exchange.;;Capacitance becomes $kC_0$, so $V=Q/(kC_0)=V_0/k$.::Use the definition of capacitance.;;$U=Q^2/(2C)$ therefore becomes $U_0/k$.::The energy formula must use the quantity held fixed.
questions.final: $V/V_0=1/k$ and $U/U_0=1/k$; energy can be released as mechanical work.

questions.prompt: Obtain the torque expression for a planar current loop. Then consider a 100-turn coil of area $2\times10^{-3}$ m² carrying 0.20 A. Its normal makes 30° with B=0.50 T. Find moment, torque and dipole energy.
questions.answer: For a rectangular loop, opposite magnetic forces of magnitude $IB\ell$ on a pair of sides form a couple. Their perpendicular separation gives $\tau=IAB\sin\theta$ for one turn, with θ the angle between its normal and B. Thus $\boldsymbol\tau=\mathbf m\times\mathbf B$, where $\mathbf m=IA\hat n$.::The Lorentz forces sum to zero in a uniform field but their moments need not cancel.;;$m=NIA=100(0.20)(0.002)=0.040$ A m².::Moments of the turns add.;;$\tau=mB\sin30^\circ=0.010$ N m.::Torque uses the angle of the normal, not the plane.;;$U=-mB\cos30^\circ=-0.0173$ J.::Choose zero dipole energy at a right angle.

questions.prompt: A very long cylinder has uniform $\mathbf M=M\hat{\mathbf z}$ and no free current. Find its bound currents and B far from its ends.
questions.answer: Uniform M gives $\mathbf J_b=0$.::Its curl is zero.;;On the curved surface, $\mathbf K_b=M\hat{\mathbf z}\times\hat{\mathbf r}=M\hat{\boldsymbol\phi}$; at flat ends the cross product is zero.::Use the outward surface normal.;;The curved sheet is equivalent to a long solenoid with surface current M.::A solenoid's current loops have the same geometry.
questions.final: $B_{\rm in}=\mu_0M$ axially and $B_{\rm out}\simeq0$, neglecting ends.

questions.prompt: Inside a block, $\mathbf M=ax\hat{\mathbf z}$. Find its volume bound current and the surface current on the face x=L.
questions.answer: Only $\partial M_z/\partial x=a$ is nonzero, so $\nabla\times\mathbf M=-a\hat{\mathbf y}$.::Use the Cartesian curl component $(\nabla\times M)_y=\partial_zM_x-\partial_xM_z$.;;At x=L, the outward normal is $\hat{\mathbf x}$ and $\mathbf K_b=aL\hat{\mathbf z}\times\hat{\mathbf x}=aL\hat{\mathbf y}$.::The cross-product order is M then n.
questions.final: $\mathbf J_b=-a\hat{\mathbf y}$; $\mathbf K_b(x=L)=aL\hat{\mathbf y}$.

questions.prompt: A long solenoid has 1000 turns/m, current 0.50 A and a linear core with $\mu_r=2$. Find H, M and B inside, and state the outside-field approximation. Recover the air-core case.
questions.answer: Ampère's law for H gives $H=nI=500$ A/m.::Only the free winding current enters.;;$\chi_m=\mu_r-1=1$, so $M=\chi_mH=500$ A/m.::Use the specified linear response.;;$B=\mu_0\mu_rH=1.257\times10^{-3}$ T.::B includes both free and bound-current effects.;;For an ideal infinitely long solenoid the exterior field is zero; far from the ends of a long real one it is approximately zero. Setting $\mu_r=1$ gives the air-core interior $B=\mu_0nI$, while $H=nI$ and M=0.::The long-solenoid approximation neglects end fringing.
tags: Prerequisite-course PYQ A26 Q16 · adapted to matter

questions.prompt: Compare P, D, M and H, and explain why $D=\epsilon_0E$ and $B=\mu_0H$ are not general material identities.
questions.answer: P is electric moment density and M is magnetic moment density.::They describe material response.;;$D=\epsilon_0E+P$ and $B=\mu_0(H+M)$.::These definitions retain both vacuum and material terms.;;Dropping P or M is justified only when that response vanishes or is being neglected.::A material can contribute substantial bound charge or current.
questions.final: In linear matter use $D=\epsilon E$ and $B=\mu H$, with specified material assumptions.

questions.prompt: Explain why a transformer core and a permanent magnet require different hysteresis behaviour.
questions.answer: A transformer cycles repeatedly, so low coercivity and a narrow loop reduce hysteresis loss.::Less irreversible rearrangement occurs each cycle.;;High permeability allows useful flux with modest excitation.::The core responds strongly to the winding current.;;A permanent magnet needs substantial remanence and high coercivity.::It must retain its state and resist unwanted demagnetization.
questions.final: Soft narrow-loop material suits transformers; hard high-coercivity material suits permanent magnets.

questions.prompt: Starting from dipole potential, derive the surface and volume bound-charge representation of a polarized object and explain its physical meaning.
questions.answer:
Let $\mathcal R=\lvert\mathbf r-\mathbf r'vert$, where r is the observation point and r′ labels source points. A volume element has dipole moment $\mathbf P(\mathbf r')d	au'$.::Polarization is moment density.;;Its potential sums to $V=(4\pi\epsilon_0)^{-1}\int\mathbf P\cdot
abla'(1/\mathcal R)\,d	au'$.::The source-coordinate gradient equals $\hat{ oldsymbol{\mathcal R}}/\mathcal R^2$.;;Apply the product rule: $\mathbf P\cdot
abla'(1/\mathcal R)=
abla'\cdot(\mathbf P/\mathcal R)-(
abla'\cdot\mathbf P)/\mathcal R$.::This moves the derivative from the distance factor to the polarization.;;The divergence theorem converts the first volume integral to a surface integral.::It equates outward flux and integrated divergence.;;Thus $V=(4\pi\epsilon_0)^{-1}[\oint\sigma_b\,da'/\mathcal R+\intho_b\,d	au'/\mathcal R]$.::These are exactly the potential formulas for surface and volume charge.;;Identify $\sigma_b=P\cdot\hat n$ and $ho_b=-
abla\cdot P$. Uniform interior P cancels there, but unmatched dipole ends remain on the surface.::This explains both the signs and the physical origin.
questions.final: The polarized object has the same macroscopic field as its equivalent bound surface and volume charges.

questions.prompt: Develop a systematic method for solving a planar dielectric interface problem with free surface charge. Include the field laws and a normal-field example.
questions.answer: Choose normal n from medium 1 into medium 2, and resolve every field into normal and tangential components.::Sign conventions prevent ambiguous jumps.;;A pillbox gives $D_{2n}-D_{1n}=\sigma_f$.::Its enclosed free charge is $\sigma_f A$.;;A tiny electrostatic loop gives $E_{2t}=E_{1t}$.::Its circulation vanishes.;;For linear isotropic media insert $D_i=\epsilon_iE_i$.::The constitutive law connects the auxiliary and physical fields.;;If the fields are purely normal, $E_{2n}=(\sigma_f+\epsilon_1E_{1n})/\epsilon_2$.::Solve the normal jump algebraically.;;For $\sigma_f=0$ and $\epsilon_2=3\epsilon_1$, $E_{2n}=E_{1n}/3$. Boundary conditions alone still need a source or far-field condition to fix its magnitude.::A relation between two unknown fields is not a complete solution.
questions.final: Use normal D and tangential E conditions together with material laws and source/geometry information.

questions.prompt: Explain how microscopic dipoles lead to M, bound currents and H. Derive the free-current Ampère law and discuss its limits.
questions.answer:
Define M as the vector magnetic moment per volume.::It averages many atomic moments.;;Microscopic loop currents cancel on internal common edges but leave a surface sheet $K_b=M	imes\hat n$; spatial variation leaves $J_b=
abla	imes M$.::These equivalent currents reproduce the macroscopic field.;;Start with $
abla	imes B=\mu_0(J_f+J_b)$.::All steady currents source the magnetic curl.;;Substitute the bound current and rearrange to $
abla	imes(B/\mu_0-M)=J_f$.::Curl is a linear operation.;;Define $H=B/\mu_0-M$ and apply Stokes' theorem to obtain $\oint H\cdot dl=I_f$.::Surface curl and edge circulation are equivalent.;;For linear isotropic matter, $M=\chi_mH$ and $B=\mu H$; in a ferromagnet this single constant law generally fails.::History and saturation change the response.
questions.final: H isolates free current in the magnetostatic circulation law; it does not erase the material's contribution to B.

questions.prompt: Compare diamagnetism, paramagnetism and ferromagnetism, including microscopic origin, field response and hysteresis.
questions.answer: Diamagnetism is an induced response opposing the applied field, with small negative susceptibility.::Orbital motion changes under the field.;;Paramagnetism aligns pre-existing moments weakly, giving small positive susceptibility.::Thermal disorder prevents complete alignment in weak fields.;;Ferromagnetism has cooperative alignment within domains.::Interactions produce order that can persist without an applied field.;;The initially weak net magnetization can grow by domain-wall motion and rotation.::Favourably oriented domains expand.;;On cycling H, pinning produces hysteresis, remanence and coercivity.::The material does not follow a unique memory-free M(H) path.;;Above the Curie temperature spontaneous order disappears; choosing a soft or hard material depends on whether repeated reversibility or retained magnetization is wanted.::Temperature and history are essential parts of the material description.
questions.final: Diamagnets oppose weakly, paramagnets align weakly, and ferromagnets show cooperative, often hysteretic response.
